name: Letters from Kali — 04 — You are allowed to change your mind
subject: You are allowed to change your mind
preheader: A writing practice for revisiting an impression without judging yourself.
label: ON DISCERNMENT · LETTER 04
title: You are allowed to change your mind.
promptStart: Return to one impression you wrote down earlier:
promptEnd: What would I understand differently now?
emphasis: Trust can include the freedom to reconsider.
body: What happens when an impression you felt strongly about doesn’t hold up?
It can be tempting to defend it, explain it away, or decide you can never trust yourself again.
There is another possibility: let the experience teach you something.
Discernment leaves room for new information. You can take an impression seriously, examine it, and change your understanding. None of those steps requires you to turn against yourself.
Writing gives you something more useful than a verdict about whether you were right. It gives you a record of what you noticed and what you learned.
Return to one impression you wrote down earlier:
What did I notice at the time?
What did I assume it meant?
What happened, and what is still unknown?
What would I understand differently now?
You may find that you noticed something real and gave it the wrong meaning. You may find that a hope or fear shaped your interpretation. You may simply need more time to know.
Trust can include the freedom to reconsider.
For this week, try replacing ‘I should have known’ with ‘What can I learn from this?’
What becomes possible when you give yourself permission to revise an impression? You’re welcome to reply.

name: Letters from Kali — 05 — A boundary can be an act of discernment
subject: A boundary can be an act of discernment
preheader: You can name what you need without claiming to know another person’s motives.
label: ON DISCERNMENT · LETTER 05
title: A boundary can be an act of discernment.
promptStart: Choose a small request or commitment you’re considering:
promptEnd: What could I say clearly and kindly?
emphasis: You can be clear about your limits while remaining uncertain about the story.
body: Sometimes the question ‘Is this intuition or fear?’ keeps us searching for a certainty we don’t yet have.
Meanwhile, a simpler question may be available: What am I willing and able to offer?
Perhaps you need more time before making a commitment. Perhaps you have reached the limit of your energy. Perhaps a request asks for more than you want to give.
You don’t need certainty about another person’s motives to name your own limits. A boundary can describe your availability without becoming a verdict about someone else.
Choose a small request or commitment you’re considering:
What is being asked of me?
What do I have the time and energy to offer?
What would I need to agree freely?
What could I say clearly and kindly?
Your answer might sound ordinary: ‘I need a day to think about it.’ ‘I can help with this part.’ ‘I’m not available this week.’
Notice whether you begin inventing a larger explanation to justify a simple need. Put that explanation on the page, too, and ask what you actually know.
You can be clear about your limits while remaining uncertain about the story.
What is one sentence you could use to name a limit this week? You’re welcome to write back.

name: Letters from Kali — 06 — Make room for a listening practice
subject: Make room for a listening practice
preheader: Bring noticing, reflection, and small steps into a practice you can return to.
label: ON DISCERNMENT · LETTER 06
title: Make room for a listening practice.
promptStart: Give yourself a few quiet minutes with these questions:
promptEnd: What small, reversible step could help me learn?
emphasis: You don’t have to turn every impression into an answer.
body: Over these letters, we’ve made room for impressions, asked questions of fear and desire, and allowed our understanding to change.
Now we can bring those questions into a practice that is small enough to keep.
Begin with one ordinary situation. Notice what arises. Write before you explain. Name what you want and what concerns you. Then consider what you can check.
Give yourself a few quiet minutes with these questions:
What am I noticing?
What am I hoping for or afraid of?
What do I know, and what remains uncertain?
What small, reversible step could help me learn?

Return to the page later. What did the step reveal? What did you misunderstand? What deserves another question? Look for patterns across several experiences rather than making one moment prove everything.
You don’t have to turn every impression into an answer.
Some impressions ask for attention. Some questions take time. A listening practice can leave room for both.
If you’d like space to explore a question through tarot and thoughtful conversation, you can learn about my private readings below.
Which question from this series would you like to keep working with? You’re welcome to reply.

name: Letters from Kali — Welcome — A place to begin
subject: Welcome to Letters from Kali
preheader: Writing, spiritual reflection, and room to ask honest questions.
label: WELCOME TO LETTERS FROM KALI
title: A little room to listen.
promptStart: If you’d like a place to begin, take a page and write:
promptEnd: One thing I’d like to understand more clearly is…
emphasis: You don’t need a finished answer to begin a conversation.
body: Welcome. I’m glad you’re here.
Letters from Kali brings together writing, tarot, and spiritual reflection: ways of exploring what we notice, the meanings we give it, and the stories we’re living.

I hold a master’s degree in creative writing from Goddard College and an undergraduate degree in psychology from the University of Tennessee. Writing belongs at the heart of this work—an invitation to observe closely and ask honest questions.

The intuition guide is sent separately after you confirm your subscription. In the letters that follow, we’ll explore discernment: how to listen to an impression while examining fear, desire, and the need to be certain.
If you’d like a place to begin, take a page and write:
One thing I’m carrying right now is…
One question I keep returning to is…
One thing I’d like to understand more clearly is…
You don’t need a finished answer to begin a conversation.
These emails will also carry invitations to readings, new writing, and gatherings as they take shape. You can unsubscribe whenever you wish.
What brought you here? You’re welcome to reply with a few words, a question, or a little of your story.

name: Letters from Kali — Retreat interest — April 2027
subject: What would you want from a writing and reflection retreat?
preheader: An overnight gathering in North Georgia is taking shape for April 2027. What would matter to you?
label: A GATHERING IN THE MAKING
title: What would make room for you?
promptEnd: What practical details would make it possible for me to attend?
emphasis: There is room to help shape this before the plans are final.
body: I’m exploring an overnight retreat in North Georgia for April 2027, bringing writing and spiritual reflection together.
The questions behind these letters would be part of it: how we listen to ourselves, how we examine fear and desire, and how writing can give us room to consider what we’re noticing.
North Georgia is the region I’m considering. The venue, exact dates, format, and price are still being worked out. I’d like to hear from people who might want to come before those decisions are made.
If this interests you, consider:
What would I most like to explore through writing and reflection?
Would I want quiet writing time, guided exercises, shared conversation, or a mixture?
Where would I be traveling from, and what travel distance would be realistic?
What practical details would make it possible for me to attend?
You can also share what price range you would be comfortable considering, if you wish.
There is room to help shape this before the plans are final.
Reply with whatever you’d like me to know. An expression of interest is not a reservation or a commitment to attend.
When there is a clear plan, I’ll share the details here.
